title: My Two Friends, This Is Azza’s Campsite
intro: Kuthayyir asks two friends to stop where Azza once camped and touch the earth that touched her skin. He remembers her oath to stay away from him and weighs his own constancy against her withdrawal. Abu Ali al-Qali records reading the poem to his teacher Ibn Durayd. The diwan sequence heard here ends with two clouds, one losing its shade and the other bringing rain just beyond the man who needs it.

translation: My two friends, here is Azza’s campsite. Hobble
your young camels, then weep where she stayed.
1.sharh: Azza has gone, but her stopping place can still be pointed out. Hobbling the animals commits all three travellers to a real stop.

translation: Touch the earth that once touched her skin.
Spend night and day where she spent hers.
2.sharh: The soil is the one thing here that has touched her. Matching the hours she passed there extends that contact through a whole day and night.

translation: Keep hoping that God will wipe away
your sins if you pray where she prayed.
3.sharh: He imagines a blessing for his companions in an ordinary patch of ground. Her prayer there is the reason the place seems special to him.

translation: Before Azza I never knew what weeping was,
or what can hurt the heart, until she turned away.
4.sharh: The man who has told his friends to weep remembers when he did not know how. Her departure taught him the meaning of his own instruction.

translation: She has hardly dealt fairly. She made other women
unlovely to me, then begrudged me her own favours.
5.sharh: She has changed his view of every other woman. Having used up the alternatives in his eyes, she gives him little of her own company.

translation: She swore her strongest oath by Him for whom
Quraysh offered sacrifice and prayed at the two passes,
6.sharh: The oath invokes the God to whom Quraysh sacrifices. Its words carry the lovers out among the pilgrims, and its pledge continues into the next verse.

translation: “I will not sit with you while pilgrims make pilgrimage
and a party at Fayfa' Al cries God’s greatness and the pilgrim call,
7.sharh: Azza’s verb means to sit together in company. The oath leaves its negative understood in Arabic. The yearly return of the pilgrims is her way of saying how long the refusal will hold.

translation: while a party above Rukba cries God’s greatness,
and at Dhu Ghazal bears the pilgrim’s sign and calls aloud.”
8.sharh: The company’s cry can be heard above Rukba. At Dhu Ghazal it takes on the outward sign of pilgrimage and raises its voice in the pilgrims’ call. Azza’s oath lasts as long as these rites recur.

translation: In cutting the cord between us she was
like a woman who fulfils a vow and is released.
9.sharh: A cord can bind people together. Here she has a competing bond, the promise she made, and fulfils it by cutting the first one.

translation: I told her, “Azza, every misfortune
grows tractable once the soul is schooled to meet it.”
10.sharh: The intimate shortened name sits beside a maxim fit for anyone. He is trying that maxim on the very loss that makes him need it.

translation: No one ever met a surge of love
that filled everything, or a blindness, without its clearing.
11.sharh: For a time passion can fill the whole field of vision. He invokes a common human history in which people eventually see their way clear again.

translation: If the talebearers ask why I broke with her,
say, “A free man’s heart was consoled and found its ease.”
12.sharh: He supplies his friends with a dignified answer for outsiders. The rest of the poem lets the listener hear what it takes to maintain that answer.

translation: When she turned away it was as if I called a rock,
a solid one where even mountain goats would slip.
13.sharh: The rock offers no answer to his voice and no purchase to a sure-footed animal. Refusal is something he can almost hear and touch.

translation: She turns away. You only meet her grudging,
and if you tire of that closeness, she tires too.
14.sharh: Even what he calls closeness comes in short supply. Once the suitor tires of asking, she makes no move to renew it.

translation: She opened a preserve no one before her had grazed
and settled valleys never occupied before.
15.sharh: A pasture reserved from grazing becomes a figure for his heart. She occupies ground to which no earlier visitor had access.

translation: If only my camel by Azza’s tent had been tethered
with a flimsy rope, badly secured, and wandered off,
16.sharh: A traveller usually wants a secure tether. Losing his transport is attractive to him because it would give him a reason to stay.

translation: and its saddle been left with the people camped there,
and someone else gone looking while she went her way.
17.sharh: He plans even for the inconvenience of searching. Let somebody else do that work, leaving the saddle, and its owner, in Azza’s camp.

translation: Then I would be like a man with two legs, one sound,
one struck by time and left paralysed.
18.sharh: He is still wishing for his camel to go astray at Azza’s camp. Staying near her would be his sound leg. Losing the animal that carries him would be the other. Ibn Hisham al-Lakhmi reads the image in light of that wish.

translation: I would be like a limping she-camel who bears down
on her lame leg after stumbling, and gets up.
19.sharh: The second lame creature has just stumbled. Its struggle to stand gives a little movement to the divided figure of the preceding line.

translation: I want to stay with her, and I suspect
that if we linger in her company she tires.
20.sharh: His own desire is certain. Her weariness is something he can only guess at, and that uncertainty spoils the visit he wishes could last.

translation: The swine makes her abuse me. She holds me
in no contempt, but submits to the man with power.
21.sharh: “The swine” is the speaker’s insult for her husband. He allows himself to believe that the abuse says more about power in her household than about what she thinks of him.

translation: May it sit well and sweet, free of any hidden sickness,
what Azza has allowed herself of my good name.
22.sharh: He wishes her the blessing said over food. The startling thing she has helped herself to is his reputation, and he would spare her even the after-effects.

translation: By God, whenever I drew close, she drew away,
breaking with me. The more I gave, the less she gave.
23.sharh: The two halves balance precisely because the lovers do not. His increased attention is met with an equal movement away.

translation: I heave sighs that would kill me if they lasted.
One follows another. My hopes have gone.
24.sharh: A sigh can pass, yet another arrives immediately behind it. His wishes have departed while the bodily strain of wishing stays with him.

translation: We had taken an uphill path in love.
When we came together there, I stood firm and she slipped.
25.sharh: For a while both lovers climbed the same slope. What might have been their meeting point becomes the place where their footing differs.

translation: We tied the knot of closeness between us.
Once we pledged ourselves, I drew it tight and she undid it.
26.sharh: The Arabic for a pledge is associated with binding. One knot makes their mutual promise tangible enough for two hands to work on it in opposite directions.

translation: If she offers reconciliation, she is warmly welcome.
It is hers by right from me, and little enough.
27.sharh: Even after describing her as the one who untied the bond, he claims no right to set a high price on making peace.

translation: If it is the other way, there are lands beyond us
that would wear out the pale camels I sent across them.
28.sharh: “The other way” is left unsaid. The distance into which he might disappear is measured in the exhaustion of the animals able to take him there.

translation: My two friends, the woman of Hajib’s line has exhausted
your two mounts, and mine too is spent.
29.sharh: The two friends from the opening return. The cost of his pursuit can now be seen in three exhausted animals.

translation: May closeness to Azza never be far, though in the end
the cords that held it have fallen away.
30.sharh: He gives the relationship the farewell one might give a person. The cords that once sustained it have already come loose.

translation: Treat me ill or well, you will have no blame
from me, nor my hatred if you turn against me.
31.sharh: The two imperatives sound like permission. What they actually offer is a promise about his own conduct under either treatment.

translation: Only give me something, and remember the affection,
the friendship we once had with you, now lost.
32.sharh: The request has grown smaller. If the old friendship cannot be given back entire, he asks that she remember it and give him something out of that memory.

translation: Though she turns away, I shall speak praise, and truth,
of the good she once did me.
33.sharh: Past generosity can still be acknowledged accurately. The word for truth gives his praise a firmer ground than the hope that it might win her back.

translation: I do not call down death on Azza,
or gloat if Azza’s sandal slips.
34.sharh: From death to a slipping sandal he names both extremes of ill fortune. Even the smallest mishap will give him no pleasure.

translation: Let the talebearers never think my yearning
for Azza was a flood that cleared away,
35.sharh: He earlier spoke as if a wave of passion must recede. He now forbids the people watching him to assume the rule applies to his love.

translation: leaving me recovered from the sickness she brought,
like a thirst-stricken camel that fell ill and then got well.
36.sharh: The denial carries over from the preceding verse. A sick camel’s recovery is precisely the outcome he refuses to claim for himself.

translation: By God, and God again, no sweetheart after her
or before her took the place she took.
37.sharh: Repeating the oath gives weight to a claim about a whole lifetime. Both before and after Azza, that place in him is hers.

translation: No day has passed for me like her day,
however great and momentous other days have been.
38.sharh: Publicly memorable days may have come and gone. His private measure of an important day still begins with the time he had with her.

translation: She settled on the highest peak of his heart.
The heart cannot forget her. The soul has never tired.
39.sharh: He briefly sees himself from outside, calling it “his” heart. Her lodging has moved from a deserted campsite to a height within the man who remembers her.

translation: How strange the heart, how it bears this,
and the soul, once schooled, coming to rest.
40.sharh: Here a rare word means patient endurance. He can come to terms with the loss of contact while going on loving her.

translation: With all my longing for Azza, now that
she and I have both let go of what lay between us,
41.sharh: Twice he speaks of letting go. The sentence hangs unfinished over the line break because the passion that remains still needs its image.

translation: I am like a man counting on a cloud for shade.
Each time he settles under it at noon, it dissolves.
42.sharh: The cloud promises relief simply by casting shade. The man has time to choose his resting place, but never to rest in it.

translation: She and I are like a cloud and a man in drought.
He hoped for it. Once it passed him, the rain came down.
43.sharh: The last cloud does deliver what it promised. The heartbreak lies in where the rain falls, just beyond the dry ground of the person who waited for it.

1.1.1.head: خَليل
1.1.1.meaning: “My two close friends”, the pair traditionally addressed at a deserted campsite.

1.1.3.head: رَبع
1.1.3.meaning: The site of a former encampment.

1.1.5.head: اِعقِلا
1.1.5.meaning: Hobble your mounts so that they stay where they are.

1.2.1.head: قَلوص
1.2.1.meaning: A young riding camel. Each companion has one.

2.2.2.head: ظِلّا
2.2.2.meaning: Spend the daytime there, paired with spending the night.

3.1.1-2.head: لا تَيأَسا
3.1.1-2.meaning: Do not give up hope. Both companions are still being addressed.

4.1.7.meaning: Weeping. The familiar Arabic noun appears here in its short form.

5.2.3.head: النَّوال
5.2.3.meaning: Something granted, here the favours of a lover.

5.2.4.head: ضَنَّ
5.2.4.meaning: To begrudge or be sparing with something.

6.1.3.head: جَهد
6.1.3.meaning: With all the force one can give an oath.

6.2.3.head: المَأزِمان
6.2.3.meaning: Al-Ma'ziman, the two narrow passes on the pilgrimage route between Arafat and Muzdalifa.

7.1.1.head: نادى
7.1.1.meaning: To sit together in company, from the word for an assembly. The oath supplies an understood negative.

7.2.1-2.head: فَيفاء آل
7.2.1-2.meaning: Fayfa' Al, a place on the pilgrims’ route. Al-Qali also transmits Fayfa' Ghazal.

7.2.4.head: أَهَلَّ
7.2.4.meaning: To raise the voice with the pilgrimage response.

8.1.5.head: رُكبَة
8.1.5.meaning: Rukba, a Hijazi place identified in one tradition as lying between Mecca and Taif.

8.2.2-3.head: ذو غَزال
8.2.2-3.meaning: Dhu Ghazal, a Hijazi stop named in the description of the pilgrims’ route.

8.2.4.head: أَشعَرَ
8.2.4.meaning: The company took on the pilgrim’s sign. The next verb, istahallat, describes the pilgrims raising their voices in response to God’s call.

9.1.2-3.head: قَطع الحَبل
9.1.2-3.meaning: “Cutting the cord”, breaking a personal bond.

9.2.4.head: أَحَلَّ
9.2.4.meaning: To be released from an obligation upon fulfilling a vow.

10.1.3-4.head: يا عَزّ
10.1.3-4.meaning: “Azza”, here shortened affectionately to “Azz” in direct address.

10.2.2.head: وَطَّنَ
10.2.2.meaning: To school or accustom oneself to something hard.

11.1.6.head: مَيعَة
11.1.6.meaning: The first rush or surge of passion.

11.2.3.head: عَمياء
11.2.3.meaning: A bewilderment in which one cannot see a way through.

12.1.3.head: الواشون
12.1.3.meaning: People who carry tales with the aim of parting lovers.

12.2.5.head: تَسَلّى
12.2.5.meaning: To find consolation or bring oneself to bear a separation.

13.2.6.head: العُصم
13.2.6.meaning: Wild goats, especially those with pale markings on the legs, proverbial climbers.

14.1.1.head: صَفوح
14.1.1.meaning: Habitually turning away or presenting only the side of her face.

15.1.2.head: حِمى
15.1.2.meaning: Reserved grazing land, used here for a part of the heart kept from others.

15.2.2.head: تِلاع
15.2.2.meaning: Watercourses running down to the floor of a valley.

16.2.3.meaning: Insecurely fastened, leaving the camel a chance to slip free.

17.1.5.head: رَحل
17.1.5.meaning: A camel’s riding saddle and frame.

17.2.3.meaning: Someone who goes looking for a strayed animal.

17.2.5.head: بَلَّ
17.2.5.meaning: To go off and wander away, the gloss al-Qali records for this line.

18.2.5.head: شَلَّ
18.2.5.meaning: To become paralysed or lose the use of a limb.

19.2.5.head: اِستَقَلَّ
19.2.5.meaning: To rise and get one’s weight back on one’s feet.

20.1.2.head: الثَّواء
20.1.2.meaning: Remaining somewhere as a guest or resident.

21.1.2.head: الخِنزير
21.1.2.meaning: “The swine”, an insult for the husband. One recension has “the jealous man”.

21.2.3.head: المَليك
21.2.3.meaning: The person with authority over her, here her husband.

22.1.1-2.meaning: “May it go down well and do you good”, a blessing said over food.

22.1.5.head: مُخامِر
22.1.5.meaning: Lodged in the body, of an illness.

24.1.2.head: زَفَرات
24.1.2.meaning: Deep sighs drawn from a troubled chest.

24.2.4.meaning: Wishes or hopes, set beside the sighs that succeed one another.

25.1.4.head: صَعود
25.1.4.meaning: A steep ascent or uphill path.

26.2.2.head: تَواثَقَ
26.2.2.meaning: To exchange pledges, each binding the other. Abbas prints tawafaqna, “we came to an agreement”.

27.1.3.meaning: Reconciliation, making amends to the person who feels a grievance.

27.2.5.head: قَلَّ
27.2.5.meaning: To count for little, here even his willingness to make peace is a small thing to give.

28.2.5.head: كَلَّ
28.2.5.meaning: To grow exhausted on the road.

29.1.3.head: الحاجِبِيَّة
29.1.3.meaning: The woman of Hajib’s line, a name for Azza through an ancestor.

29.1.4.head: طَلَّحَ
29.1.4.meaning: To wear out a mount by long travel.

30.2.1.head: بِعاقِبَة
30.2.1.meaning: At last or in the end.

30.2.2.head: أَسباب
30.2.2.meaning: Cords, then the ties that sustain a relationship.

32.1.2.meaning: Grant a favour or some share of your company.

33.2.5.head: أَزَلَّ
33.2.5.meaning: To confer a kindness or bestow a benefit.

34.2.4-6.head: زَلَّتِ النَّعل
34.2.4-6.meaning: “Her sandal slipped”, any stumble, mistake or misfortune.

35.2.3.head: غَمرَة
35.2.3.meaning: A flood or an overwhelming spell.

36.1.5.head: دَنَف
36.1.5.meaning: A wasting sickness, often applied to lovesickness.

36.2.3.head: هَيماء
36.2.3.meaning: A camel suffering from a disease of unquenchable thirst.

37.2.4.head: خُلَّة
37.2.4.meaning: A beloved companion, here a woman dear to him.

40.1.5.head: اِعتِراف
40.1.5.meaning: Patient endurance under adversity, an older sense recorded by al-Qali.

41.1.2.head: تَهيام
41.1.2.meaning: An extreme, wandering passion or infatuation.

42.2.3.head: المَقيل
42.2.3.meaning: A rest in the midday heat, or the place chosen for it.

43.1.4.head: مُمحِل
43.1.4.meaning: A person whose land is suffering drought.

43.2.4.head: اِستَهَلَّ
43.2.4.meaning: Of a cloud, to begin pouring rain.
